extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, practitioners, and students concerned with judicial review of agency rulemaking and notice-and-comment procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and normative proposal about whether courts should permit post hoc rationalizations by agencies in hard-look (arbitrariness) review, revising the Chenery explanation requirement to reduce ossification and delay while preserving substantive constraints on agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery explanation requirement (no post hoc rationalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative order cannot be upheld unless the grounds upon which the agency acted in exercising its powers were those upon which its action can be sustained; courts must judge the propriety of agency action solely by the grounds invoked by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from SEC v. Chenery Corp.; courts uniformly reject agencies supplying alternate explanations during litigation. Historically justified as a foundation of administrative law and a basis for reversal when agencies fail to articulate the basis for decisions. Courts treat post-hoc rationalizations skeptically and often remand when the agency's original rationale is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bowman leniency — uphold if agency's path reasonably discerned
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts may not supply a reasoned basis the agency itself has not given, they will uphold an agency decision of less-than-ideal clarity if the agency's path may reasonably be discerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Bowman Transportation v. Arkansas-Best; allows some judicial lenity in reading less-clear agency explanations, permitting upholding where the rationale can be reasonably inferred from the record, but does not permit wholesale post hoc fabrication of new justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept explanations that 'illuminate implicit' reasons; reject 'entirely new theory'
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may accept subsequent explanations that merely illuminate reasons obscured but implicit in the administrative record, but will reject post hoc explanations that advance an 'entirely new theory' not implicit in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and cases (e.g., Consumer Fed'n v. HHS) draw the line: additional background or clarification may be acceptable, but novel theories introduced in litigation are disallowed; courts distinguish between illuminating implicit rationales and creating new bases for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to specify policy premises, reasoning, and factual support
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must articulate the policy premises, their reasoning, and factual support for regulatory decisions; over time courts have demanded increasingly detailed explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally Chenery demanded minimal explanation, but doctrine developed to require specification of policy premises and factual support so the reviewing court can discern and evaluate the agency's rationale. Failure to provide such detail has been a frequent ground for remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on considering statutorily irrelevant factors (Overton Park rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not be allowed to consider factors that are statutorily irrelevant to their decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Citizens to Preserve Overton Park; this remains a constraint on agency rationales even under proposals to permit post hoc explanations. Courts must ensure that any permissible rationale is not grounded on factors irrelevant under the governing statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error approach to agency explanations (APA §706 'prejudicial error')
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency's original explanation is inadequate, courts might treat the deficiency as harmless error and uphold the rule if a permissible rationale can be discerned from the record or if the error is unlikely to have altered the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogized to the harmless-error doctrine in criminal appeals; §706's instruction to take due account of prejudicial error could provide a statutory basis for weakening Chenery. Applied in some administrative cases, but courts have been cautious; adopting this risks incentivizing sloppy explanations unless courts carefully differentiate plausible from implausible post hoc rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate-review analogy for alternative rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts often affirm lower-court decisions even if they rely on different or additional rationales than the lower court provided; by analogy, courts could sustain agency actions based on alternative rationales that are supportable by the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chenery distinguished administrative review from appellate practice, but the Note argues the distinction is weak: appellate practice permits formulation of alternative grounds, and similar deference could reduce remand-driven delays while still respecting limits on judicial intrusion into agency domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal: allow limited post hoc rationalization (constrained to record and litigation positions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts ought to allow agencies to proffer alternative justifications during litigation and uphold regulations when a reasonable rationale can be discerned from evidence in the administrative record or litigation positions, without otherwise loosening other doctrinal constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal recommends a return to a less rigorous Chenery conception: courts would credit rational connections between facts and choice ex post, akin to harmless-error review or appellate affirmation, but limited to justifications grounded in the existing record or positions taken in litigation; it does not alter requirements to avoid statutorily irrelevant factors or to consider alternatives where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing decision costs (delay and ossification) against error costs
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to require strict ex ante explanations, courts (and scholars) should balance the welfare losses from delay and ossification caused by remands against the welfare losses from permitting potentially erroneous regulations to stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Scenic Hudson (lost project), National Coalition Against the Misuse of Pesticides, and American Textile; empirical studies suggest many remanded rules are implemented within ~2 years and agencies recover ~80% of the time, so remand costs (delay, ossification, deterrence of beneficial regulation) are a significant factor in evaluating Chenery's desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex ante explanation as disciplining/signaling device ('sunlight' theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring agencies to explain policies publicly ex ante may discipline agencies and improve policymaking via public debate and signaling the quality of decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invokes Brandeis's 'sunlight' aphorism, Judge Friendly's view that Chenery forces agencies to 're-think' questionable rules, and Stephenson's signaling theory: the quality of an explanation can serve as a screen for regulation desirability even when judges lack technical expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that permitting post hoc rationalization incentivizes strategic inadequate explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: If courts will supply or credit post hoc rationales, agencies might strategically give inadequate explanations initially to cut corners or for political reasons, expecting courts to conjure acceptable justifications later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to harmless-error incentives in criminal law; mitigation depends on judicial ability to distinguish plausible from implausible ex post rationales and on procedural safeguards to deter intentional under-explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain other doctrinal limits despite relaxing Chenery (no change to requirements to consider alternatives or avoid irrelevant factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if post hoc rationalization is allowed, other aspects of hard-look review—such as requirements that agencies consider alternatives where law requires and not base decisions on statutorily irrelevant factors—should remain intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal explicitly does not alter whether agencies must consider alternatives or the Overton Park prohibition; it limits its scope to permitting courts to credit reasonable ex post rationales grounded in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern about judicial ideological influence in arbitrariness review
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard-look arbitrariness review outcomes are influenced by judges' politics; judicial review doctrines should account for the risk of politicized decisions by judges who may be overwhelmed or guided by their own values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites empirical findings (Miles & Sunstein) showing ideological voting in hard-look cases; suggests that awareness of ideological tendencies or institutional design (e.g., panel composition) might be used to mitigate politicized invalidations if Chenery is relaxed.
